videos.title: 7 Tax Deductions and Credits Most People Forget to Claim
videos.intro: Every year, millions of Americans leave money on the table because they never claim tax breaks they qualify for. In this video, we walk through seven of the most commonly missed deductions and credits, in plain English. A quick note first: this is general information, not personal tax advice, and the rules and income limits change, so always confirm the details on irs.gov or with a tax professional.

points.head: The Earned Income Tax Credit
points.text: The Earned Income Tax Credit is a refundable credit for low and moderate income workers, and it is one of the most valuable tax breaks in the country. Refundable means that if the credit is bigger than the tax you owe, you can still get the difference as a refund. The IRS estimates that a share of eligible people never claim it, often because they are not required to file a return. If you worked and earned a modest income, check the IRS eligibility tool, because the amount depends on your income, filing status, and number of qualifying children.

points.head: The Saver's Credit
points.text: If you contribute to a retirement account like a 401k or an IRA and your income is within the limits, you may qualify for the Saver's Credit. It can be worth up to fifty percent of the first two thousand dollars you contribute, and it comes straight off your tax bill, which is better than a deduction. Many people who qualify have never heard of it, because it is claimed on Form 8880 and tax software only asks about it when you answer the right questions.

points.head: Student loan interest
points.text: If you paid interest on a qualified student loan, you may be able to deduct up to twenty five hundred dollars of it, and you can take this deduction even if you do not itemize. Your lender will send you a Form 1098 E if you paid at least six hundred dollars in interest. The deduction phases out at higher incomes, so check the current limits for your filing status.

points.head: Education credits
points.text: Two credits help with college costs. The American Opportunity Credit is worth up to twenty five hundred dollars per student for the first four years of college, and part of it can be refundable. The Lifetime Learning Credit is worth up to two thousand dollars per return and can be used for graduate school or classes to improve job skills. You cannot claim both for the same student in the same year, so compare them before you file.

points.head: Medical expenses
points.text: If you itemize, you can deduct the part of your unreimbursed medical and dental expenses that is more than seven and a half percent of your adjusted gross income. That sounds like a lot, but in a year with surgery, braces, or a long illness, the total can add up. Keep your receipts, insurance statements, and even a log of mileage to medical appointments.

points.head: Child and dependent care credit
points.text: If you pay for child care or care for another dependent so that you can work or look for work, you may qualify for the child and dependent care credit. It is a percentage of your care costs, up to a limit per dependent. You will need the care provider's name, address, and tax identification number, so ask for it when you pay, not months later.

points.head: Health Savings Account contributions
points.text: If you have a high deductible health plan, a Health Savings Account gives you a rare triple tax advantage. Contributions are tax deductible, the money grows tax free, and withdrawals for qualified medical expenses are tax free too. Many people with a qualifying plan never open an account, or forget to report contributions made outside of payroll. Unused money rolls over every year, so it can also work like an extra retirement account for medical costs.

videos.outro: That is seven tax breaks that people commonly miss: the Earned Income Tax Credit, the Saver's Credit, student loan interest, education credits, medical expenses, the child and dependent care credit, and Health Savings Account contributions. Which one surprised you the most? Check the details at irs.gov or ask a tax professional, and subscribe to TaxSaveUSA for more practical money and tax tips every day.

videos.title: 7 Mistakes That Trigger IRS Penalties (And How to Avoid Them)
videos.intro: IRS penalties are some of the most avoidable costs in personal finance, yet they catch millions of people every year. In this video, we cover seven common mistakes that lead to penalties and interest, and the simple habits that prevent them. This is general information, not personal tax advice, so confirm the details for your situation on irs.gov or with a tax professional.

points.head: Filing late
points.text: The penalty for filing late is much bigger than the penalty for paying late. If you owe tax and file after the deadline, the failure to file penalty is generally five percent of the unpaid tax for each month, up to twenty five percent. Even if you cannot pay everything, file on time. The IRS also offers payment plans, which cost far less than ignoring the problem.

points.head: Thinking an extension gives you more time to pay
points.text: Form 4868 gives you an automatic extension to file, usually until October, but it does not give you more time to pay. Interest and the failure to pay penalty, which is generally half a percent of the unpaid tax per month, start from the original due date. If you request an extension, estimate what you owe and pay as much as you can by the April deadline.

points.head: Underpaying during the year
points.text: The United States has a pay as you go tax system. If you are self employed, earn investment income, or have side income without withholding, you may need to make quarterly estimated payments. To avoid an underpayment penalty, a common safe harbor is paying at least ninety percent of this year's tax or one hundred percent of last year's tax. If your income was higher, the prior year figure can be one hundred and ten percent. Employees can also fix this by adjusting the Form W 4 at work.

points.head: Income that does not match
points.text: The IRS receives copies of your W 2s, 1099s, and other forms, and its systems compare them to your return. If you forget a 1099 for freelance work, interest, or a brokerage sale, you will probably get a notice. Before you file, gather every form, check your online IRS account, and report all income, even if you did not receive a form.

points.head: Small errors on the return
points.text: Wrong Social Security numbers, a misspelled name, math mistakes, and incorrect bank account numbers delay refunds and cause notices. File electronically with direct deposit, because software catches many errors for you, and double check every number you type, especially your routing and account numbers.

points.head: Ignoring IRS letters
points.text: Almost every IRS notice has a deadline printed on it. Ignoring a letter does not make it go away, it usually makes the amount larger and shortens your options. Read it carefully, compare it to your return, and respond by the date given. If you agree, pay or set up a plan. If you disagree, send your documents in writing, and consider asking a tax professional for help.

points.head: Not keeping records
points.text: Generally, the IRS can audit a return for three years after you file it, and longer in some cases. Keep copies of your returns and the records that support every deduction and credit, like receipts, mileage logs, and statements. Digital copies are fine. Good records are your best protection if you are ever asked to prove a number.

videos.outro: To recap: file on time, remember that an extension does not extend payment, pay enough during the year, report all of your income, double check your return, answer IRS letters quickly, and keep good records. Do these seven things and you avoid most penalties. For more simple tax and money tips, subscribe to TaxSaveUSA.

videos.title: How to Get Your Tax Refund Faster: 6 Things That Actually Work
videos.intro: Waiting for a tax refund can feel like forever, especially when you are counting on that money. The good news is that a few simple choices make a real difference in how fast it arrives. In this video, we cover six things that actually work, based on how the IRS processes returns. This is general information, not personal tax advice.

points.head: File electronically
points.text: An electronically filed return is processed much faster than a paper one. A paper return has to be opened, scanned, and typed in by hand, which can take weeks or even months. The IRS says that most e filed refunds are issued in less than twenty one days. If you can e file, do it.

points.head: Choose direct deposit
points.text: Direct deposit is the fastest and safest way to receive your refund. A paper check has to be printed and mailed, and it can be lost, stolen, or delayed. Type your routing and account numbers slowly and check them twice, because a single wrong digit can send your refund to the wrong place or hold it up for weeks.

points.head: Get the details exactly right
points.text: Most delays come from small errors. Names must match your Social Security card, the numbers must be right, and every form must be attached. If you moved or changed your name, update your records first. Software helps by checking for common mistakes before you submit.

points.head: Know the rules for certain credits
points.text: By law, the IRS cannot issue refunds that include the Earned Income Tax Credit or the Additional Child Tax Credit before mid February. If you claim one of these credits, filing early still helps, because the IRS can start processing, but the money will not arrive until after that date.

points.head: Track it the right way
points.text: Use the Where's My Refund tool on irs.gov or the IRS2Go app. You need your Social Security number, your filing status, and the exact refund amount from your return. The tool updates once a day, so checking more often does not help. Calling the IRS usually does not speed anything up unless the tool tells you to.

points.head: Do not wait to file
points.text: If you are owed a refund, there is no reason to wait until the deadline. File as soon as you have all of your tax forms. Just make sure you have every document first, because filing too early without a form and then fixing it later with an amended return is slower than waiting a few days to file it correctly the first time.

videos.outro: So the plan is simple: e file, use direct deposit, double check every detail, understand the credit rules, track your refund on irs.gov, and file once you have all of your documents. If you found this useful, subscribe to TaxSaveUSA for more clear tax tips.

videos.title: Self-Employed Taxes Explained: 7 Things Every Freelancer Must Know
videos.intro: Working for yourself is great, but the tax rules are different from having an employer, and surprises can be expensive. In this video, we explain seven things every freelancer, gig worker, and small business owner should know. This is general information, not personal tax advice, so verify details on irs.gov or with a tax professional.

points.head: You pay self employment tax
points.text: When you work for yourself, you pay both halves of Social Security and Medicare tax. That is called self employment tax, and the rate is fifteen point three percent on most of your net earnings. It is on top of regular income tax. You can deduct half of it when you calculate your adjusted gross income, which softens the blow.

points.head: Quarterly estimated payments
points.text: No one withholds tax from freelance income, so the IRS expects you to pay during the year. Estimated payments are made four times a year, using Form 1040 ES or your IRS online account. A good habit is to move a percentage of every payment into a separate savings account the day you get paid, so the money is there when the due date comes.

points.head: Track every business expense
points.text: You are taxed on your profit, not your total income, so every legitimate business expense lowers your tax. Common ones include software, supplies, phone and internet used for business, professional fees, and advertising. Keep receipts and use a separate bank account and card for business so it is easy to prove what is business and what is personal.

points.head: The home office deduction
points.text: If you use part of your home regularly and exclusively for your business, you may be able to deduct a portion of home costs. There is a simplified method that uses a flat rate per square foot, and a regular method that uses actual expenses. The key words are regularly and exclusively, so a desk in the corner of the living room where the family watches television may not qualify.

points.head: Mileage and vehicle costs
points.text: If you drive for business, you can deduct either the standard mileage rate or your actual vehicle costs. The standard mileage rate is set by the IRS every year. The most important thing is a written log with the date, destination, purpose, and miles for every trip, kept at the time of the trip, not rebuilt at tax time.

points.head: The qualified business income deduction
points.text: Many sole proprietors, partners, and owners of pass through businesses can deduct up to twenty percent of their qualified business income. There are limits based on income and the type of business, but for many small business owners this deduction can be significant. It is taken on your personal return, so make sure your software or preparer applies it.

points.head: Retirement and health insurance
points.text: Self employed people have no employer plan, but there are options that also reduce your tax. A SEP IRA or a Solo 401k lets you put away a large part of your profit, and contributions are generally deductible. You may also be able to deduct health insurance premiums that you pay for yourself and your family, if you meet the requirements.

videos.outro: To recap: expect self employment tax, make quarterly payments, track your expenses, look into the home office and mileage deductions, claim the qualified business income deduction if you qualify, and use retirement and health insurance deductions. Organize your records now and tax time becomes much easier. Subscribe to TaxSaveUSA for more tax and money tips every day.

videos.title: 4 New Tax Deductions for 2025 to 2028: Tips, Overtime, Car Loans, Seniors
videos.intro: Four new federal deductions are available for tax years 2025 through 2028, and many people have not heard about them. In this video we walk through each one, using figures from the IRS. This is general information, not personal tax advice.

points.head: No tax on tips
points.text: The IRS says you can deduct up to 25,000 dollars of qualified tips. It starts to phase out when modified adjusted gross income is above 150,000 dollars, or 300,000 dollars for joint filers. If you are self employed, the deduction is capped at the net income from that business.

points.head: No tax on overtime
points.text: You can deduct up to 12,500 dollars of qualified overtime pay, or 25,000 dollars if you file jointly. The same income thresholds apply, starting at 150,000 dollars, or 300,000 dollars for joint filers.

points.head: Car loan interest
points.text: Up to 10,000 dollars of qualified passenger vehicle loan interest can be deducted. The phase out starts above 100,000 dollars of modified adjusted gross income, or 200,000 dollars for joint filers. There are rules about the vehicle and the loan, so check the IRS guidance and your lender's interest statement.

points.head: The senior deduction
points.text: If you are 65 or older, you may be able to deduct an extra 6,000 dollars, or 12,000 dollars if both spouses qualify. It begins to phase out above 75,000 dollars of income, or 150,000 dollars for joint filers.

points.head: You do not have to itemize
points.text: The IRS says these deductions are available whether you itemize or take the standard deduction. That makes them useful for a lot of people who normally just take the standard deduction.

points.head: What to do now
points.text: Keep your pay stubs, tip records, and loan interest statements. Then read the IRS pages on the Working Families Tax Cuts before you file, so you know exactly which rules apply to you.

videos.outro: So there are four deductions to remember: tips, overtime, car loan interest, and the senior deduction. Check the IRS page for the full rules. If this helped, subscribe to TaxSaveUSA for more clear tax tips.

videos.title: 2026 IRS Numbers Cheat Sheet: Standard Deduction, Brackets, Credits
videos.intro: The IRS has published its 2026 inflation adjusted numbers. In this video we go through the figures most people need: the standard deduction, tax brackets, the zero percent capital gains rate, and a few credits. This is general information, not personal tax advice.

points.head: Standard deduction
points.text: For 2026 it is 16,100 dollars for single filers, 24,150 dollars for head of household, and 32,200 dollars for married couples filing jointly.

points.head: Tax brackets for single filers
points.text: The 12 percent bracket goes up to 50,400 dollars of taxable income, and the 22 percent bracket goes up to 105,700 dollars. These are marginal rates, so only the dollars inside each bracket are taxed at that rate.

points.head: Zero percent capital gains
points.text: Long term capital gains can be taxed at zero percent if your taxable income is at or below 49,450 dollars for single filers, 66,200 dollars for head of household, or 98,900 dollars for married couples filing jointly.

points.head: Earned Income Tax Credit
points.text: The maximum credit is 664 dollars with no qualifying children, 4,427 dollars with one child, 7,316 dollars with two children, and 8,231 dollars with three or more.

points.head: Commuter benefits
points.text: The monthly limit is 340 dollars for transit passes and commuter vehicles, and 340 dollars for qualified parking.

points.head: Adoption credit
points.text: The maximum credit for 2026 is 17,670 dollars of qualified expenses, and it starts to phase out when modified adjusted gross income passes 265,080 dollars.

videos.outro: Those are the main 2026 numbers from the IRS. Always check irs.gov for the figures that apply to your situation. If this helped, subscribe to TaxSaveUSA for more clear tax tips.

videos.title: How Wealthy People Legally Lower Their Taxes (7 Strategies)
videos.intro: Wealthy families do not break rules, they use them. In this video we walk through seven strategies anyone can learn from, from retirement accounts to charitable giving. This is general education, not personal advice.

points.head: Max out tax advantaged accounts
points.text: The 2026 limits are 24,500 dollars for a 401k and 7,500 dollars for an IRA. Traditional contributions lower this year's taxable income, and Roth contributions grow tax free.

points.head: Use the health savings account
points.text: Contributions are deductible, growth is tax free, and medical withdrawals are tax free. For 2026 the limits are 4,400 dollars for self only and 8,750 dollars for family coverage.

points.head: Hold investments longer than a year
points.text: Long term capital gains are taxed at 0, 15, or 20 percent, which is usually well below ordinary income rates.

points.head: Harvest your losses
points.text: Investment losses offset gains, and up to 3,000 dollars of extra loss can offset regular income each year.

points.head: Give appreciated stock
points.text: Donating shares you have held more than a year can avoid the capital gains tax and may still earn a deduction if you itemize.

points.head: Use depreciation
points.text: Rental property owners can deduct the cost of a building over 27 and a half years, which can shelter rental income.

points.head: Plan the estate early
points.text: The 2026 federal estate tax exemption is 15 million dollars per person, and the annual gift exclusion is 19,000 dollars per recipient.

videos.outro: Those are the key points. This is general education only, not personal tax advice, so confirm details on irs.gov or with a tax professional. If this helped, subscribe to TaxSaveUSA for more clear money and tax tips.

videos.title: Tax Credits And Rebates You May Be Missing In 2026
videos.intro: Credits cut your tax bill dollar for dollar, and millions go unclaimed every year. Here are the ones worth checking for 2026. This is general information, not personal advice.

points.head: Earned Income Tax Credit
points.text: The maximum for 2026 is 664 dollars with no children and up to 8,231 dollars with three or more children, depending on income.

points.head: Child Tax Credit
points.text: The new law sets the credit at 2,200 dollars per qualifying child under 17, and it is indexed for inflation after that.

points.head: Saver's Credit
points.text: Up to 1,000 dollars, or 2,000 for couples, for contributing to a retirement account, if your income is under 40,250 dollars single or 80,500 joint.

points.head: Child and Dependent Care Credit
points.text: Pays back a share of childcare costs that let you work. Also look at the dependent care FSA, which rises to 7,500 dollars in 2026.

points.head: Education credits
points.text: The American Opportunity Credit is worth up to 2,500 dollars per student, and the Lifetime Learning Credit up to 2,000 dollars per return.

points.head: Adoption credit
points.text: For 2026 it covers up to 17,670 dollars of qualified adoption expenses.

videos.outro: Those are the key points. This is general education only, not personal tax advice, so confirm details on irs.gov or with a tax professional. If this helped, subscribe to TaxSaveUSA for more clear money and tax tips.

videos.title: Self-Employed Tax Savings: Deductions Freelancers Miss
videos.intro: Working for yourself means more control over your taxes, and more deductions to claim. Here are the biggest ones. This is general education, not personal advice.

points.head: Qualified business income deduction
points.text: Many pass through business owners can deduct up to 20 percent of qualified business income, and the new law made it permanent.

points.head: Solo 401k or SEP IRA
points.text: You can shelter far more than an employee. The overall limit for 2026 is around 72,000 dollars, with catch up contributions if you are 50 or older.

points.head: Home office deduction
points.text: Use the simplified method at 5 dollars per square foot up to 300 square feet, or deduct actual expenses with the regular method.

points.head: Mileage and vehicle costs
points.text: The 2026 business mileage rate is 72.5 cents per mile. Keep a log, because the IRS expects one.

points.head: Health insurance and HSA
points.text: Self employed people can often deduct health insurance premiums, and an HSA adds another deduction if you have a qualifying plan.

points.head: Half of self employment tax
points.text: You can deduct the employer equivalent half of your self employment tax, which lowers your income tax.

points.head: Estimated taxes
points.text: Pay quarterly. The safe harbor is 90 percent of this year's tax or 100 percent of last year's, or 110 percent if your income was over 150,000 dollars.

videos.outro: Those are the key points. This is general education only, not personal tax advice, so confirm details on irs.gov or with a tax professional. If this helped, subscribe to TaxSaveUSA for more clear money and tax tips.

videos.title: Roth vs Traditional: Which Saves You More Tax?
videos.intro: The Roth versus traditional question is one of the biggest money decisions you will make. Here is how to think about it. This is general education, not personal advice.

points.head: The basic difference
points.text: Traditional contributions are deducted now and taxed when you withdraw. Roth contributions are taxed now and withdrawn tax free.

points.head: Compare tax brackets
points.text: If you expect a higher bracket in retirement, Roth usually wins. If you expect a lower one, traditional often wins.

points.head: 2026 limits
points.text: You can contribute 24,500 dollars to a 401k and 7,500 dollars to an IRA, with higher catch up amounts at 50.

points.head: Roth IRA income limits
points.text: For 2026 the phase out is 153,000 to 168,000 dollars single and 242,000 to 252,000 joint.

points.head: Backdoor Roth
points.text: High earners can contribute to a traditional IRA and convert it, but the pro rata rule can create a tax bill.

points.head: Diversify
points.text: Many people use both, so that in retirement they can choose which bucket to draw from to manage their bracket.

videos.outro: Those are the key points. This is general education only, not personal tax advice, so confirm details on irs.gov or with a tax professional. If this helped, subscribe to TaxSaveUSA for more clear money and tax tips.

videos.title: Government Programs That Save You Money: Subsidies And Help
videos.intro: Many families qualify for help they never claim. Here are real programs that can lower your bills. Eligibility varies, so always check the official sites. This is general information.

points.head: LIHEAP
points.text: The Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program helps with heating and cooling bills. Each state runs its own program, so find yours through acf.gov or by calling 211.

points.head: Weatherization Assistance
points.text: Eligible households can get free insulation and air sealing to cut energy bills. Find your state contact at energy.gov.

points.head: Lifeline
points.text: Takes up to 9.25 dollars a month off phone or internet service for qualifying households. Apply at lifelinesupport.org.

points.head: Pell Grants
points.text: Free college money you do not repay. The maximum is 7,395 dollars a year. Apply through the free FAFSA at studentaid.gov.

points.head: Medicare Savings Programs
points.text: Can pay Medicare Part B premiums for people with limited income. Ask your state Medicaid office.

points.head: Free tax help
points.text: VITA volunteers prepare federal returns for free for people with moderate incomes, and can help you claim credits you might miss.

videos.outro: Those are the key points. This is general education only, not personal tax advice, so confirm details on irs.gov or with a tax professional. If this helped, subscribe to TaxSaveUSA for more clear money and tax tips.

videos.title: Real Estate Tax Benefits: Why Property Owners Pay Less
videos.intro: Real estate has some of the most powerful tax benefits in the code. Here is how they work. This is general education, not personal advice.

points.head: Mortgage interest deduction
points.text: Interest on up to 750,000 dollars of home loan debt is deductible if you itemize. Mortgage insurance premiums are deductible again starting in 2026.

points.head: Property taxes and the SALT cap
points.text: The cap on state and local tax deductions is 40,400 dollars for 2026, phasing down for incomes above 505,000 dollars.

points.head: Home sale exclusion
points.text: If you owned and lived in your main home for two of the last five years, you can exclude up to 250,000 dollars of gain, or 500,000 for couples.

points.head: Rental depreciation
points.text: Residential rental buildings are depreciated over 27 and a half years, which can offset rental income.

points.head: 1031 exchange
points.text: Investors can defer capital gains tax by rolling proceeds into another like kind investment property, following strict deadlines.

points.head: Step-up in basis
points.text: Heirs generally receive property at its value on the date of death, which can erase the built in gain for income tax.

videos.outro: Those are the key points. This is general education only, not personal tax advice, so confirm details on irs.gov or with a tax professional. If this helped, subscribe to TaxSaveUSA for more clear money and tax tips.
